opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so my bias, and I think it's a healthy one, is to start embarrassingly simple. The first model I want to see on any new problem is something like a linear model or logistic regression on reasonable features, or maybe a random forest or gradient boosted trees if the data is tabular. Part of that is practical: those models are fast, they're hard to mess up, and they give you a baseline in an afternoon instead of a week. But the bigger reason is that a simple model tells you something about the problem itself. If logistic regression gets you ninety percent of the way there, that's a very different project than if it's barely above chance.

The other thing a simple baseline does is help you debug your *data*, which is usually where the real problems are. If a dead-simple model does suspiciously well, you probably have leakage. If it does terribly, maybe your labels are noisy, or your train/test split doesn't reflect how the model will actually be used. You want to find those things out before you've invested in a big architecture, because otherwise you can't tell whether a failure is the model's fault or the data's fault.

After that, I try to match the model to the structure of the data. That's really where the leverage is. If your data has a natural symmetry or a natural representation, you want an architecture that respects it. Images have translation invariance, so convolutions made sense. Sequences, you think about recurrence or attention. When I was working on molecules and smell, molecules are naturally graphs: atoms are nodes, bonds are edges, and the properties shouldn't depend on how you happen to number the atoms. So graph neural networks were a pretty obvious thing to reach for, and they did turn out to be a big step up over hand-engineered molecular fingerprints. But we only knew how big a step because we'd run the fingerprint-plus-random-forest baseline first.

And then the last piece is just being honest about your evaluation before you fall in love with any model. Decide what metric actually matters, and set up a split that reflects how the model will really be used. For molecules, for example, a random split can be very misleading because similar molecules land in both train and test, so you want something like a scaffold split. If you get that right up front, model selection becomes almost mechanical: you try the simple thing, you try the thing that respects the structure of your data, and you let the honest benchmark tell you which one to keep investing in.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly recommends starting with an embarrassingly simple model and gives linear models, logistic regression, and tree models as initial choices.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I try to start with the simplest thing that could possibly work, and I mean that quite literally. Before I touch a neural network, I want to know what a linear model does on the problem, or even just what the mean of the training labels gets me. That baseline is doing real work for you. It tells you how hard the problem actually is, and it catches the embarrassing bugs, like a leaky feature or a mislabeled column, before you've spent a week tuning hyperparameters on something that's broken underneath.

The second thing I ask is what the structure of the data is, because that usually narrows the field a lot. If there's a strong prior in the data, like translation invariance in images or sequence structure in text or molecules, I want a model family whose inductive biases match that. In the olfaction work, for instance, a molecule is naturally a graph, so graph neural networks were the obvious place to start, not because they're fashionable but because they encode the right assumptions about what matters. Fighting the structure of your data with a generic model is just making your life harder.

And then I try to be disciplined about moving up the ladder of complexity only when the simpler model gives me a reason to. If a gradient-boosted tree on hand-crafted features is within a few percent of the fancy model, that's a really important signal, and often it means the bottleneck is the data or the labels, not the architecture. The models that look impressive on day one are rarely the ones that teach you the most about the problem. The cheap, boring ones usually do.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly recommends starting with “the simplest thing that could possibly work,” beginning with a linear model or label-mean baseline before trying a neural network.

astra-6.text:
I like to start with the simplest thing that could possibly work. Before picking a model, I want to understand the data, what we’re trying to predict, and how we’ll know whether we’re doing a good job. What’s the baseline? Could you get surprisingly far by predicting the most common outcome, or by using a handful of features and a linear model?

That first model is really a way to test your understanding of the problem. You can look at its mistakes, see where your assumptions break down, and check whether your evaluation actually measures what you care about. Then you have a reason to add complexity. If you jump straight to a very complicated model, you’re changing so many things at once that it’s hard to know what you’ve learned.

r001.rationale: The response says to start with “the simplest thing that could possibly work” and suggests a common-outcome baseline or a linear model before adding complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I usually start by asking, what’s the simplest thing we can try that will tell us whether there’s signal in the data? That might be a linear model or a small neural network. The goal is to get the whole loop working: the data, the model, and an evaluation that actually reflects what we care about.

Once you have that baseline, you can make more informed choices. Look at where it fails. Is the model missing something important, or are the labels noisy? Do you need a different representation, or more data? I’d rather let those experiments guide the complexity than start with the most sophisticated model available.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting with the simplest useful model, giving a linear model or small neural network as examples.
